## Introduction

This page covers how the shell finds the programs you run (the `$PATH`),
and how you can make lasting changes to your shell's settings
using configuration files like `~/.bashrc`.

_To run the commands on this page yourself, start a VS Code session at_
_<https://ondemand.osc.edu> in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`._

## `$PATH`: where the shell looks for programs

### What is the `$PATH`?

`$PATH` is an environment variable like `$HOME` and `$USER`,
which you learned about in [week 3](../week03/w3a_shell-basics.qmd).
It contains a list of directories,
and whenever you type the name of a program,
the shell searches these directories for an executable file with that name.
This is why you can run programs without specifying the full path to their executable.

To see where the executable for a command is located,
you can use the `which` command:

```bash
which nano
```
```bash-out
/usr/bin/nano
```

<!-- TODO: check the output above at OSC -->

To check which directories are in your `$PATH`, you can simply `echo` it:

```bash
echo $PATH
```

<!-- TODO: add current OSC output (bash-out block) -->

That output is hard to read,
because the directories are separated by colons `:`.
Let's make it a bit more readable by replacing the colons with newlines
(`tr ":" "\n"`), and numbering the lines (`nl`):

```bash
echo $PATH | tr ":" "\n" | nl
```

<!-- TODO: add current OSC output (bash-out block), possibly truncated -->

The order of the directories matters:
the shell searches them from first to last,
and runs the **first** matching executable that it finds.

### Modules and Conda change your `$PATH`

In [week 6](../week06/w6b_software.qmd), you saw that the `fastqc` command
is not available until you load its module.
Now you can understand what `module load` does: it adds the directory with
FastQC's executable to the start of your `$PATH`:

```bash
which fastqc
```

<!-- TODO: add OSC output: "no fastqc in (...)" -->

```bash
module load fastqc/0.12.1
which fastqc
```

<!-- TODO: add OSC output: path to the module's fastqc executable -->

Activating a [Conda environment](conda.qmd) works the same way.

### Changing your `$PATH`

You can add a directory to your `$PATH` by assigning a new value to the variable
that consists of the old value (`$PATH`), a colon, and the new directory:

```bash
# Add a dir to the END of the $PATH:
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"

# Or add a dir to the START of the $PATH:
export PATH="$HOME/software/bin:$PATH"
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Some notes on the above commands _(Click to expand)_

- `export` makes a variable available to programs that you run from your shell.
  `$PATH` is already exported, so `export` is not strictly needed here,
  but it is customary to include it.

- We use `$HOME` rather than `~` because the shell does not expand `~`
  inside double quotes.

- Don't forget the `$PATH` part! If you were to run `PATH="$HOME/software/bin"`,
  the shell would no longer find basic commands like `ls`.
  If this happens, simply open a new terminal to start over.
:::

Like any variable you set in the shell,
this change only affects your **current shell session**.
To make it permanent, you'll need to add the line to a configuration file
--- see [below](#shell-configuration-files).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Running your own scripts like any other command _(Click to expand)_

In [w7a](../week07/w7a_scripts1.qmd), you saw that a script in your working dir
needs to be run as `./script.sh` when you don't use `bash script.sh`.
If you put scripts with execute permissions in a directory that is in your `$PATH`,
you can run them from anywhere just by typing their name, e.g.:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/software/bin
cp scripts/fastqc.sh ~/software/bin
chmod +x ~/software/bin/fastqc.sh
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"

# You can now run the script from any directory without specifying its path:
fastqc.sh
```

For scripts that belong to a specific research project, though,
it is better to keep them within the project dir and run them from there.
:::

<br>

## Shell configuration files

### `~/.bashrc` and `~/.bash_profile`

Your Bash shell is configured by hidden text files in your Home dir.
The two most important ones are:

- `~/.bash_profile`, which is read by **login shells**:
  the shell that you get when you first log in to a computer,
  e.g. with `ssh`.
- `~/.bashrc`, which is read by **non-login interactive shells**:
  shells that you start after you're already logged in,
  e.g. when you open another terminal.

To avoid having to deal with this distinction,
it is common to put all your settings in `~/.bashrc`,
and to have `~/.bash_profile` run `~/.bashrc`.
This is often already set up by default, which you can check as follows:

```bash
cat ~/.bash_profile
```

If the output contains a line like `. ~/.bashrc` or `source ~/.bashrc`
(typically within an `if` statement),
then `~/.bash_profile` runs `~/.bashrc`, and you only need to edit `~/.bashrc`.

### What to put in your `~/.bashrc`

To see what's currently in your `~/.bashrc`,
use `cat` or open the file in VS Code:

```bash
cat ~/.bashrc
```

Some things that you can store in this file:

- Changes to your `$PATH`, like the one in the [previous section](#changing-your-path).
- Other environment variables, like the `$APPTAINER_CACHEDIR` variable
  from [week 6](../week06/w6b_software.qmd#the-container-image-cache-storage).
- Aliases: your own shortcuts for commands --- see [below](#aliases).
- The look of your prompt.

You can add a line to your `~/.bashrc` by editing it in VS Code,
or by appending a line with `echo` and `>>`:

```bash
echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/software/bin"' >> ~/.bashrc
```

::: callout-warning
#### Use single quotes with `echo` here!
With double quotes, the shell would replace `$PATH` with its _current_ value
before the line is written to the file.
Single quotes make sure that the line is written exactly as shown,
so that `$PATH` is expanded each time the file is read instead.
:::

Changes to your `~/.bashrc` take effect in **new** shells.
To apply them to your current shell as well, run:

```bash
source ~/.bashrc
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Some precautions when editing your `~/.bashrc` _(Click to expand)_

- Make a backup before making changes:

  ```bash
  cp ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc_backup
  ```

- A mistake in your `~/.bashrc` can cause errors every time you open a shell.
  If that happens, fix or remove the problematic line,
  or restore your backup.

- Use `>>` to append, and not `>`, which would overwrite the entire file!
:::

<br>

## Aliases

An alias is a custom shortcut for a command.
You create one with the `alias` command,
followed by the alias name, an equals sign, and the full command in quotes:

```bash
alias ll='ls -lh'
```

From now on, typing `ll` will run `ls -lh`.
You can also add further options and arguments when you use an alias:

```bash
ll -a data/
```

To see all aliases that are currently defined, run `alias` without arguments.
Some aliases may already be defined by default ---
for example, `ls` is often an alias for `ls --color=auto`.

As with changes to your `$PATH`,
aliases only last for the current shell session,
unless you add them to your `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
echo "alias ll='ls -lh'" >> ~/.bashrc
```

::: callout-note
#### Don't use aliases in scripts
Aliases are a convenience for working interactively.
They are not available in scripts by default,
so always write out the full commands in scripts.
:::

<br>
